newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: US defence chiefs urge caution in helping N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: US defence chiefs urge caution in helping N.Korea.

text.p: Top U.S. defence officials on Friday cautioned against rushing to help North Korea, saying the nation was on a war footing despite its appeals for food to avert famine and may not be ready for peace.
Defence Secretary William Cohen and the chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, General John Shalikashvili, injected stern warnings into growing international sympathy for North Korea's plight.

Cohen portrayed a repressive government cynically begging for food while pouring scarce resources into a military ready to strike South Korea "at a moment's notice" with chemical weapons and Scud missiles.
He made clear large-scale assistance was unlikely unless Pyongyang began dismantling its military machine and showed it was ready to repay food with goodwill peace gestures.

"I doubt very much whether there will be massive assistance without some kind of reciprocal action on the part of the North Koreans," he told reporters before leaving South Korea at the end of his first trip to Asia as defence secretary.
Shalikashvili questioned how badly the North really was hurting, saying fighter pilots had increased their flying time and the military had just completed extensive winter drills.

"If they are in such great difficulty as they claim they are and if they are in need of assistance, why are they spending their resources on this kind of military exercising, you have to ask yourself," he told reporters in Tokyo after a visit to South Korea.
The stony comments contrasted with heart-wrenching descriptions of hunger and depravation by U.S. congressmen and international aid workers who recently visited the country.

Coming just five days before North Korea has said it will respond to an offer for peace talks, the officials appeared to be setting the stage for tough bargaining over the terms of Pyongyang's participation.

Pyongyang officials have demanded substantial food aid before joining talks between the two Koreas, the United States and China aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.

"There is still scepticism as to whether or not North Korea is prepared to pursue a path of peace as opposed to simply trying to procure additional food to keep its citizenry fed while its military continues to function and to soak up what limited resorces they have," Cohen said.
"It would be unreasonable to expect the world community to subsidise and support a domestic economy that is in a state of collapse while the military continues to operate at ordinary rates."
He warned Pyongyang any aggression would be suicidal, resulting in "overwhelming damage and defeat" for the Stalinist state. The United States maintains 37,000 troops in the South.
Earlier, Pyongyang demanded South Korea apologise over a shooting incident that occurred along the border on Thursday, shortly before Cohen flew to another part of the frontier.

U.S. and South Korean officials said Southern border guards fired warning shots at a group of North Korean soldiers who had crossed the border line. The communist soldiers replied with shots into the air before pulling back.

"South Korea should apologise for having obstructed the normal patrol work of the People's Army and endangered their lives and they should take steps that this will never happen again," Pyongyang radio said.

The U.N. World Food Programme has appealed for $95.5 million for 200,000 tonnes of food for North Korea, well short of what is needed to stave off famine in North Korea, devastated by two consecutive years of floods.
Asked about further aid, Cohen said: "Much will depend on what kind of progress is made as far as peace talks is concerned."
